newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Malaysia courts, criticises fund managers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malaysia courts, criticises fund managers.

text.p: Malaysia appears to have a dual message to foreign fund managers and analysts: come, but watch what you say about our economy and markets.
Facing a bearish stock market and slower growth after property and stock loan curbs and spillover sentiment from Thailand's economic crisis, Malaysian officials have been hitting back at critics.

The actions of hedge funds and currency speculators, able to move markets with huge inflows of foreign capital, have also been in the spotlight after regionwide upsets in the foreign exchange markets.
Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, never shy about criticising Western influences, blasted "rogue speculators" for undermining southeast Asian economies.

"We want to embrace borderlessness but we still need to protect ourselves from self-serving rogues and international brigandage," he told the 30th anniversary meetings of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) in July.
Early in July, Deputy Finance Minister Wong See Wah said fund managers in industrialised countries were disseminating inaccurate economic analyses of even countries with sound economic fundamentals.
And just two months before that, Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange president Salleh Abdul Majid in a newspaper column lambasted a local television station for airing "inaccurate" market views "too often".
He even singled out Yamaichi Advisory Services managing director Katsuhiko Abe for his "very gloomy and negative picture" of the Malaysian share market.
COURTING FOREIGN FUND MANAGERS

All this may seem unremarkable since most countries would prefer to hear positive, rather than negative, views. But amidst the carping about unflattering comments, Malaysia is busily courting foreign fund managers to build up a fledgling asset management industry.

Its Securities Commission (SC) has unveiled several rounds of new regulations meant to unshackle the asset management industry and encourage its growth, including allowing 10 joint venture foreign fund management firms to manage domestic unit trust funds.
Such joint ventures would tap outside expertise "in circumstances where in-house fund management capabilities cannot be propertly developed", the SC said last December.

Still, Malaysia has not followed the actions of neighbour Thailand, which after its currency bloodbath in July, raided the offices of several foreign brokers to find out the origins of a fax speculating the closure of some Thai banks.
VALUE FOR CLIENTS
Malaysia's public attacks on foreign analysts have raised some eyebrows in the investing community.

"Stock markets go up and stock markets go down," said a foreign fund manager. "At the moment, the Malaysian stock market is down. Fund managers are looking for value for their clients. That's what I look for."
Since the end of March, when the central Bank Negara Malaysia clamped down on loans for property and stocks, the Composite Index representing 100 key blue chips has shed about 13 percent.
Compared with economies like Thailand's which has been showing the slowest growth in a decade, Malaysia is faring much better and should be evaluated on its own, fund managers say.

"I think at the end of the day, they (foreign analysts) may have overshot themselves on their criticisms of Malaysia," another foreign fund manager said. "But that's the way capital markets work sometimes. The pendulum can swing against you."
INVESTOR CONCERNS

Abe, the Yamaichi analyst who was singled out for criticisms, said in May that his comments on the market reflected investor concerns when they heard Mahathir was going away on an unprecedented two-month holiday.
"It's not only me, but everybody...I didn't say it to push down the market," Abe told Reuters the day the column ran.
A local fund manager said that while some foreign analysts' reports on Malaysia have been inaccurate, "I don't think it warrants the public scolding of managers."

For now, analysts may choose to lie low, until Malaysia's financial markets find their bearings, fund managers said. But, the criticisms are unlikely to keep foreign investment interest completely out of Malaysia, they added.
"They (foreigners) are going to be watching things very carefully," a foreign fund manager said.
"If they (the government) bring in measures to control capital flows, that will send panic in the market. Short of that, Malaysia will be looked at on a fundamental basis."
